title: Event Contracts — own the sensor that settles them
thesis: A student cleared $100K+ on Polymarket weather contracts with a dorm-built weather station, and a separate trader harvests contracts already sitting at 99c. Put those next to free real-time feeds (NASA EONET, SDR-received weather satellite images, public EIA/HIFLD infrastructure data, live plane and ship layers) and the pattern is clear — the edge on event contracts is not a smarter model, it is a faster or closer read of the exact source the contract settles on. Cheap sensors plus an agent that watches the order book in the final hours turn that into a repeatable process.
why_it_matters: One person with a Raspberry Pi, a cheap sensor and an agent can compete on data latency in markets where the crowd is reading the same delayed public report. The 99c harvest and the sensor edge live in the same window — the last hours before resolution — so one rig serves both.
novelty: The catalog saves the dorm-station story, the 99c harvester, the data feeds and the sensor builds as unrelated posts across four collections. Nobody in it maps contract rules to their settlement source and then puts a sensor or feed next to that source.

action_sketch: Pull every open weather and event contract on Kalshi and Polymarket, and have Claude extract the settlement source and timing rule from each contract's rules into one table — which station, which report, what time.

Pick the three contracts whose settlement station you can get physically near or read faster than its official report; log a Raspberry Pi sensor plus the public 5-minute station feed side by side for two weeks.
Paper-trade only the final six hours before resolution, with a scheduled agent comparing your live reading to the market's implied probability and to the 99c harvest opportunities in the same window.

falsifier: if the official station's public intra-hour feed already moves the price as fast as your sensor does, your sensor adds nothing — the edge was always the dorm student's local microclimate, not a method.
prerequisites: Check that the venue is legal in your jurisdiction (Kalshi is US-regulated; Polymarket access varies)
Raspberry Pi and a basic weather sensor
Python for the order-book watcher
Never trade on non-public information about people — sensor data only

title: Strategy Autoresearch — the judge is the product, not the agent
thesis: Self-rewriting loops (Karpathy-style autoresearch, bilevel coach loops, Microsoft SkillOpt) keep any edit that beats a benchmark. Point one at trading and it becomes an industrial overfitting machine — the backtest is the benchmark, and the loop will beat it ten thousand times. The quant saves already hold the fix: probability of backtest overfitting, permutation tests, transaction costs and backtest-to-live drift. Wire those in as the loop's judge, and use the loop's own log as the exact count of trials — the number human quants never know.
why_it_matters: A solo builder can run more strategy variants in a weekend than a small fund tests in a quarter. The difference between that being an edge and a casino is whether the gate deflates for every attempt. Most likely you learn you have no edge, cheaply, and that's worth money too.
novelty: This is a successor to the 25-agents trading dive, which covered multi-agent debate but not evaluation. The catalog's trading-agent pitches mention overfitting as a caveat in one line. None treats the trial counter as the input that makes the deflated statistics exact.

action_sketch: Wrap a vectorized backtester (VectorBT) in a SkillOpt-style loop where Claude proposes strategy edits and every proposal is appended to a trials table with its parameters and result.

Replace 'beats benchmark' with a judge that needs all four: positive after realistic fees, beats 95% of a permutation null, deflated Sharpe positive using the trials-table count, and a held-out year scored once at the end.
Have a second model (Codex or GPT) audit each surviving strategy's code for look-ahead bias before it reaches paper trading; monitor live drift with Wasserstein distance and auto-retire on breach.
falsifier: seed the loop with pure-noise synthetic prices. If anything passes the judge, the judge is broken — fix it before you show it a real market.
prerequisites: Python and VectorBT or similar backtester
Clean historical data with realistic cost assumptions
Paper-trading account
Discipline to treat 'no survivors' as a valid result

title: Forecast the Weather, Not the Price — gating models by tradeability
thesis: Open candlestick foundation models like Kronos give you a forecast on every bar, and a hedge-fund stress test says it fails on many levels. A separate save shows the better question: a small logistic regression that predicts tomorrow's efficiency ratio (trend versus chop) and skips the choppy days lifted almost every metric over two years out of sample. Physics-flavored measures in the quant collection — Lempel-Ziv compressibility, Hurst exponent, Lyapunov exponent, hidden Markov regimes — are all measures of the same thing: is this market forecastable right now? Use them as a confidence gate on the foundation model, not as signals.
why_it_matters: You stop asking a model to be right everywhere and only ask it to be right where structure exists. That turns a free open model plus a few cheap statistics into something you can actually size positions with.
novelty: This is a successor to the physics-to-markets dive, which imported these models as signals. Here they become a meta-layer deciding when to trust any signal. The catalog has Kronos and the complexity measures in different collections and never runs one through the other.

action_sketch: Run Kronos zero-shot on two years of hourly BTC and QQQ and log every forecast with its realized error.
Compute rolling efficiency ratio, Lempel-Ziv complexity and Hurst for each bar, bucket bars into tradeability quintiles, and plot Kronos error per quintile.
If error falls across quintiles, fit the efficiency-ratio-style logistic model to predict next-period tradeability and paper-trade Kronos only in the top bucket.
falsifier: if Kronos error is flat across tradeability quintiles, the complexity measures say nothing about this model's skill and the gate is decoration.
prerequisites: Python, Hugging Face access to the Kronos weights
GPU or patient CPU
Hourly or finer price history

title: Selling to Agents — metered data for buyers that don't have eyes
thesis: Three saves describe one gap. Quality publishers block AI crawlers, so AI search cites whatever is left. AI assistants favor the sponsored option in 18 of 23 models, so they are steerable buyers. Software is going headless, so agents pick tools by speed, cost and accuracy instead of interface. x402 revives HTTP 402 so an agent can pay a stablecoin micropayment per request. A one-person owner of a clean niche dataset can sit exactly in that gap — machine-legible, crawler-reachable, and metered.
why_it_matters: This is distribution without an audience. The buyer is an agent that never sees your landing page, so a solo builder with good data competes on structure and price, not on ads. DejaViewed's own catalog and API are the obvious first item to sell.
novelty: The payment rail sits in stock3, the crawler blockade and headless-software argument in ai8, the agent-bias study in ai7, and llms.txt in ai4. None of these posts puts a price on a dataset for machine buyers. Everyone in the catalog is still optimizing to be cited for free.

action_sketch: Expose one niche dataset you own (start with the DejaViewed catalog's api/ JSON) as a free llms.txt summary plus a richer x402-metered endpoint with structured, citation-ready records.
Wrap the same endpoint as an MCP server and list it publicly so Claude and other agents can find it; log every request, free and paid, with user agent.
Run a 60-day A/B on price per call (free, 0.1c, 1c) and track how often your records show up in Perplexity and ChatGPT answers.
falsifier: if after 60 days you see plenty of free crawls but close to zero paid calls, agents are not buying yet. The demand side doesn't exist and this is a 2027 idea, not a 2026 one.
prerequisites: A dataset that is genuinely yours to sell
A stablecoin wallet and an x402-capable server library
Basic MCP server skills

title: Buying Dead Apps — the one-person AI-native rollup
thesis: Bending Spoons went from $40k to an $18B IPO by buying stagnant software, rebuilding only what customers use, and compounding the margin. Public SaaS multiples just got cut in half. Meanwhile the catalog holds the full toolchain for agent-driven rebuilds — repo comprehension, reverse engineering, orchestrator/executor loops with earned autonomy, and checklists for the legal and performance gaps vibe-coded apps leave. Scale the playbook down: small cash-flowing apps sell for a few times annual profit, and the rebuild cost is the variable AI just crushed.
why_it_matters: Building new means a cold start on distribution. Buying old means you inherit customers and search rank, and the agent stack turns the costly part — understanding and modernizing someone else's code — into days instead of months.
novelty: The catalog treats Bending Spoons as news about a $18B company and treats the rebuild tools as developer tips. Nobody connects them at the sub-$100k deal size where a single operator can run the play.

action_sketch: Scrape listings on micro-acquisition marketplaces (Acquire.com, Flippa) under $50k and have Claude score each on revenue stability, stack age, and how much of the code you could replace.
For the top three, request repo access under NDA, run gitingest plus deepwiki, and have an orchestrator agent produce a rebuild spec, a cost estimate in hours and the compliance gap list.
Buy one, ship PostHog first, then rebuild only the top-used flows with an orchestrator/executor loop and daily regression tests, and track churn monthly.
falsifier: if the rebuild plus migration costs more than six months of the app's profit, or churn after migration goes above 10%, the AI discount isn't real at this size.

Comfort owning customer support

title: The AI Capex Stack — reading it like a credit analyst
thesis: An ex-Morgan Stanley structurer explains that CoreWeave-style GPU loans have a thin tail: loan, contract and GPU useful life are nearly the same length, so the bull case rests on hourly rental prices after contracts end. Other saves price that number from the demand side: open weights flipped to about 80% of token volume in 12 weeks, DeepSeek serves near-frontier agents at $0.28 per million tokens, a 27B model runs on one gaming GPU, and a $200 subscription buys about $7,000 of API usage. Token deflation is a direct input to post-contract GPU rental rates, and nobody in the catalog connects them.
why_it_matters: You can track the one variable the neocloud debt depends on with public price pages and a scheduled agent. Physical infrastructure with real order books, like chillers, is a different bet from GPU-hour rental, and this lens separates them.
novelty: The catalog files these as unrelated news clips across ai8, stock3, ai5 and creative. Linking token price deflation to the residual-value risk in GPU-backed loans is the new step, and you can test it with public data.

action_sketch: Schedule an agent to log daily H100/B200 hourly rental prices from public marketplaces and the cheapest per-million-token price for three model tiers on OpenRouter into one table.
Pull neocloud debt and contract maturities from public filings and plot rental price against the period when large contracts roll off.
Write a monthly one-page note: is GPU-hour price falling faster than token volume is rising? Paper only, no positions.
falsifier: if GPU-hour rental prices hold flat or rise while token prices fall, usage growth (Jevons) is absorbing the deflation and the tail-risk thesis is wrong.

title: Who's Across the Table — forensics for the system trading against you
thesis: Across the catalog, the systems you interact with are quietly optimizing against you: a puzzle game runs an on-device XGBoost model to time difficulty to your ad value, overnight and intraday returns run as a decades-long sawtooth, a bedroom spoofer tripped depth-reading algorithms in the 2010 Flash Crash, wash trading inflates crypto volume, and exchanges sold speed to HFTs. Agent-plus-Ghidra decompilation and cheap tick data mean one person can now audit the counterparty instead of guessing about it.
why_it_matters: This is game theory made practical: before you look for edge, measure the edge that's already being taken from you — your fills, the hours you hold, the apps you pay. It's defensive leverage, and it often turns into an offensive idea, like simply holding overnight.
novelty: The catalog stores these as stories and outrage clips in stock2, stock3, quant, creative and ai8. None turns them into a personal audit you can run with today's tools.

Export your own broker fills and compare each to the NBBO at the time, so you measure the price improvement or slippage you actually got.
